title: Francis, again
tomorrow: who stays up all night talking with an innkeeper, and why?

cards: Clearing out a closet can feel like losing something, or like finally breathing. In Assisi, a cloth merchant's son has been giving his father's money to the poor and to a crumbling church.

The father hauls him before the bishop to get it back. And the son, Francis, does more than return the money. Thomas of Celano, who wrote his life, says he took off his clothes, right there, and handed them back too.
The bishop covered him with his own cloak.

teach.b: Why? Because Francis wanted nothing standing between him and God, not even a father's name stitched into his clothes. And his poverty wasn't grim.
He wrote the Canticle of the Creatures, praising God through brother sun, sister moon, even sister death.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.
teach.b: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Francis took that literally and lightly at once. Where did the gladness come from?

In his Testament, Francis says that while he was still in his sins, the sight of lepers was bitter to him. Then the Lord led him among them, and what had seemed bitter turned into sweetness of soul and body.
Giving up the distance came first. The joy came after. The one to tell a friend: Francis wrote the Canticle in his everyday Italian, not in Latin, and it's a song of thanks, not of loss.
Poor and glad: empty hands, and room to receive.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Francis of Assisi on October 4, often with blessings of animals; Franciscan friars and sisters take a vow of poverty and pray his Canticle of the Creatures.

o: the saint who gave everything back, and sang
a missionary who sailed to Asia to preach
a pope who wrote about caring for creation

games.q: the week, and Francis — tap the pairs.
p: theirs is the kingdom of heaven

s: Francis gave up his things because he thought the world was bad
he praised God through brother sun and sister moon. his poverty was glad, not grim.
Francis gave his clothes back to his father in front of the bishop
Thomas of Celano tells it; the bishop covered him with his own cloak.
Aquinas taught that grace replaces your nature
this week's line: grace perfects nature, it doesn't destroy it.

games.q: you're Francis, standing before the bishop. your father wants his money back. what do you do?
o: give back the money, and the clothes too.
argue that the money was rightly given away.
promise to pay it back slowly from your wages.
games.why: Celano says he handed back the money and stripped off his clothes as well, and the bishop wrapped him in his own cloak.

practice: Reach for one thing within arm's length that you could live without, and set it to one side, ready to give away. Then hold your empty hand open for the rest of the sit.
If you pray, you can thank God for one thing you already have, the way Francis thanked him for the sun.

wordCard.voice: Francis. The merchant's son from Assisi who gave everything back, and sang.

orig.note: medieval Italian, written in Latin letters: praised be you. the refrain of Francis's Canticle of the Creatures.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: poor and glad, empty hands with room in them for what God gives next. Another week, done.
